persona.who: 71, retired engineer in Fremont, came to the US in 1979. Wife passed last year. Goes to the temple, volunteers. Grandkids don't speak much Hindi.
persona.note: Lost my wife of 44 years in March. I do the temple seva, I keep busy. But the evenings. I want to understand what the Gita actually says about where she is now, not what people tell me to make me feel better.

understanding.bridge: The evenings are where the Gita speaks of what does not pass: the self that was your wife, and the truth that nothing that is real is ever lost.
understanding.week_thesis: The text does not make the loss smaller, but it gives you something real to hold in the evenings: the self that was your wife, which no death can take.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the loss and the search, and that you want the text's own word, not consolation.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the search is for what does not pass, and the Gita's answer is that what is real is never lost.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the self that was your wife is not gone because the body is gone.
week_beats.act: You read the teaching on the self that does not die, and sit with the truth in the evenings.
week_beats.story: A king who lost everything and was taught what does not pass shows you what to hold when all else is gone.

understanding.core_struggle: A retired man who lost his wife of years in March, wants to understand what the Gita says about where she is now.
understanding.insight: The ache is this big because your love was this real. Grief is love that has nowhere left to go.

situations.label: I want to reconnect with my roots
Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

queries.hook: A loss that does not pass, and a search for what the texts say about where she is now, beyond what anyone offers to make the pain smaller.
queries.diagnose: Grief is love with nowhere to go; everything that comes together must part, and the heart aches because the bond was real.
queries.steady: What is real in a person cannot be taken by death; the self is not born and does not die, and what was your wife is not gone.
queries.act: Read the teaching on the self that does not die, and sit with the truth that what is real in her is not gone, even when the evenings are empty.
queries.story: A king who lost his father and his kingdom, who asked the same question and was taught what does not pass.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.sanskrit: वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहायनवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि । तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
verse.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.
verse.misuse: Not a way to brush off someone else's grief with 'they've just changed clothes'.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, who has laid down his bow and is broken by the sight of his own family arrayed against him. He is asking what is real, and what is left when everything he loves is about to be destroyed. Krishna says that the self inside us is never born and never dies. It simply leaves this worn-out body and enters another, just as we take off an old shirt and put on a new one.
verse.for_you: You have laid down your routine and are looking for what is real beneath the loss of your partner. In the quiet of your evenings, you can let go of the worn-out shape of your days and rest in the truth that the self which was your partner has not been destroyed by March.

verse.speaker: Kausalya
verse.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
verse.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
verse.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
verse.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
verse.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

verse.meaning: In the Ayodhya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Kausalya speaks to Dasharatha. She has just lashed out at him over Ram's exile, and now she apologises. She tells him that grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. It destroys your learning, and it destroys everything. She says there is no enemy like it. The verse proposes that sorrow can make us wound those we love, and that apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.for_you: The evenings bring a heaviness that makes the past feel sharper and the future harder to see. When that happens, you might notice your mind turning over the same sharp words you wish you had said, or the same moments you want to undo. Grief wears away your steadiness.

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Yama on the self within changing bodies.
verse.sanskrit: अशरीरँ शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् । महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
verse.line: Knowing what stays steady inside all that changes, the wise do not grieve.
verse.translation: Knowing the self as bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.
verse.why: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

prasang.title: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

verse.meaning: Yama tells the boy Nachiketa that the true self is bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading. The wise one does not grieve. He says the self is never born and never dies, not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
verse.for_you: In the quiet of the evening, the ache is real because your love was real. But the self that was your partner is not gone. Nothing that is real is ever lost. Hold onto this truth as you sit with your grief.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
verse.sanskrit: गुणैः संवेष्टितो देहस्तिष्ठत्यायाति याति च । आत्मा न गन्ता नागन्ता किमेनमनुशोचसि ॥
verse.line: The body comes and goes; what you truly are does not. Why grieve so?
verse.translation: The body, made of nature's qualities, comes, stays and goes. The Self neither comes nor goes. Why grieve for it?
verse.why: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.
verse.misuse: Grief is natural; this offers perspective, not a rule against mourning.

prasang.title: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka. He tells him that the body is made of changing elements, so it is born and it dies. But the true Self is not born and does not die. It simply stays. Ashtavakra asks why Janaka would grieve for what only changes, when the core of who he is remains untouched by time.
verse.for_you: In the evenings, the quiet makes the loss feel final. But the body that held your partner is only a vessel. The truth is that the core of who they were, the awareness they shared with you, is not gone. It stays.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
verse.sanskrit: क्वासे क्व च गमिष्यामि कोऽन्वहं किमिहास्थितः / कस्मात्किमनुशोचेयमित्येवं स्थापयेन्मनः
verse.line: In grief, ask: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I? Let that steady you.
verse.translation: 'Where was I before? Where will I go? Who am I, really, and why am I here? Why should I grieve, and for what?' Ask these, and steady the mind.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
verse.misuse: These questions are for steadying grief, not for dismissing it; mourning is natural.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth. Ashma says that pain comes from what we did not want or what we lost, that meetings end and days do not return, and that we should ask where we came from, where we are going, who we are, and why we are here. Then steady the mind, and hold to the people still in front of you.
verse.for_you: Let yourself grieve, honour them by living well, and remember that the self they loved in you, and in them, does not perish.

verse.speaker: Narada
verse.setting: The sage Narada comforts the young Shuka with a teaching on grief and contentment.
verse.sanskrit: निमेषमात्रमपि हि वयो गच्छन्न तिष्ठति / स्वशरीरेष्वनित्येषु नित्यं किमनुचिन्तयेत्
verse.line: Life doesn't pause, not even for the blink of an eye. Don't spend it brooding.
verse.translation: Not even for the blink of an eye does life stand still. In a body that is passing, why brood as if things last forever?
verse.why: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

prasang.title: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

verse.meaning: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and sees him lost in grief. He tells him that life never pauses, not even for an instant. In a body that is passing, there is no point in brooding as if things will last forever. Brooding does not heal pain, it only makes it grow. The mind is healed by understanding, just as the body is healed by medicine.
verse.for_you: The temple seva and the daytime keep the hours moving. In the evening, the stillness returns and the mind wants to circle the same loss. This verse asks you to guard the mind as you would the body. Do not let the evening hours become a place of brooding.

story.title: The sixteen kings: Narada consoles Srinjaya
story.story_hook: A king could not stop weeping for his son, so a sage began telling him about everyone else who had died.
story.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira how Narada consoled King Srinjaya, whose son had died, by recounting sixteen legendary kings far greater than his son who also died. Moved, Srinjaya listens, and Narada restores the boy.
story.lesson: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.

anchor.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
anchor.speaker: Narada (retold by Krishna)
anchor.setting: Narada consoles King Srinjaya, whose only son has died, by telling of sixteen great kings who also died.
anchor.sanskrit: सुखदुःखैरहं त्वं च प्रजाः सर्वाश्च सृञ्जय / अविमुक्ता मरिष्यामस्तत्र का परिदेवना
anchor.line: You, I and everyone will die, all of us still mixed with joy and sorrow. You're not alone in this.
anchor.translation: Srinjaya, you, I and all creatures will die without being freed from joy and sorrow. So why such lament?
anchor.why: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.
anchor.misuse: It is not telling a grieving parent to stop crying; the story ends with the son restored.

prasang.story_hook: A king could not stop weeping for his son, so a sage began telling him about everyone else who had died.
prasang.lesson: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.

script: The evenings have grown very heavy for you since March. You are sitting with a loss that still feels too new to hold, and your mind keeps circling the same question about where your partner has gone. You are searching for something solid to stand on.

Arjuna has laid down his bow on the battlefield. He is looking at his own family lined up against him, and he is broken. He asks Krishna what is real and what is left when everything he loves is about to be destroyed. And Krishna replies:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहायनवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि, तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही.
In plain words: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.

Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, who has laid down his bow and is broken by the sight of his own family arrayed against him. He is asking what is real, and what is left when everything he loves is about to be destroyed. Krishna says that the self inside us is never born and never dies. It simply leaves this worn-out body and enters another, just as we take off an old shirt and put on a new one.

In the quiet of your evenings, you can let go of the worn-out shape of your days. You do not have to solve the whole puzzle tonight. You only have to let the truth rest with you: the self which was your partner has not been destroyed by March.
What would it feel like to hold that one truth gently, without trying to fix the rest?

depth.life: You sit in the quiet of the evening after two hours on the phone, the house holding the shape of your partner's absence. You are trying to hold on to what is real, searching for a truth that can sit beside you in this new stillness.
depth.points: The self is not the body that leaves. What you loved in your partner is not a garment that can be worn out. The truth is that the real self never departs, it only moves into what is new.
depth.practice: Place your hand on your chest and feel the steady breath there, knowing this is the same self that was your partner and that nothing real is ever destroyed.
depth.question: What would it feel like to let the evening hold this truth instead of the ache?
